A white speech bubble with black outline near the top left. Inside the bubble the text reads: "Every advance is the same trick: abstraction." panels.bubble_text: Every advance is the same trick: abstraction.
panels.speaker: COSMOS

panels.text: There is a single idea connecting everything in this issue — and in the entire history of computing. That idea is abstraction. Abstraction means hiding complexity behind a simpler interface. You don't need to understand an engine to drive a car. Each layer of technology abstracts away the details beneath.

panels.caption: The abstraction ladder: every layer hides the complexity below

panels.text: The essential insight: no rung replaces the ones below it. Your browser still runs on machine code. FORTRAN still compiles to assembly. The abstraction ladder is not a replacement chain — it's a stack. And the stack only works because every layer faithfully translates to the one beneath it.

panels.prompt: An international academic conference room in the late 1950s, a diverse group of European and American mathematicians and computer scientists gathered around a table covered with papers and notation, a blackboard behind them shows formal grammar notation with arrows and brackets labeled BNF, the atmosphere is intellectual and intense, men in tweed jackets and dark suits, cigarette smoke curling upward, warm amber and sepia tones, comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes

panels.text: Around the same time, an international committee designed ALGOL (ALGOrithmic Language). It introduced Backus-Naur Form (BNF) for describing grammars and block structure for organizing code. ALGOL never dominated commercially, but its ideas shaped every language that followed — making it arguably the most influential language of the era.

panels.lab_description: See the abstraction ladder in action! Type real code and watch it transform through four layers — from source code down to binary — with mapping lines showing how each element corresponds across levels.

panels.text: Abstraction is the superpower of computing. Each layer hides complexity and lets humans think at a higher level. But no layer works alone — they all rest on the layers beneath. The entire history of programming is the story of building this ladder, one rung at a time.
FORTRAN was for math. COBOL was for business. But a mathematician at Dartmouth had a wilder question: could a programming language teach machines to THINK?
